newsitem.title: USA: CompUSA says Christmas sales weak, sees hope.
newsitem.headline: CompUSA says Christmas sales weak, sees hope.

text.p: CompUSA Inc Chief Executive Officer James Halpin said he was "not happy" with sluggish Christmas retail sales but predicted the release of Intel Corp's new multimedia chip in January would bring better business.
"Retail sales in the last two weeks of December were soft and that caused a little bit of disappointment, but things go forward," Halpin told Reuters in an interview.
Halpin said he thought Christmas sales were slow because customers preferred to wait for the January 8 introduction of Intel's new multimedia MMX chip before upgrading their computers.

"We think our corporate customers and a lot of our retail customers are waiting for that chip to come out on January 8," Halpin said, playing down concerns that the MMX technology might not have attracted sufficient publicity to drive a new wave of computer upgrades.
"The technical people, the corporate customers and heavy computer users certainly understand it," he said.
CompUSA earlier reported a disappointing 1.5 percent increase in same-store sales in the second quarter of fiscal year 1997, which ended December 28.
Most analysts had expected a rise in same-store sales of about three percent, and CompUSA's shares dropped five to 15-5/8 on the New York Stock Exchange in early afternoon trade.
Halpin said the sluggish retail sector was hurting CompUSA less than its competitors and that he was "cautiously optimistic" about business in the coming months.

"You saw Best Buy lose money last quarter and you saw Tandy closing up Incredible Universe and about 20 Computer City stores, and we continue to take market share," Halpin said. "While I'm not happy with sales, I am certainly pleased with the way our business continues to run."
Halpin said he expects computer retailers to tone down the aggressive promotions seen in the run-up to Christmas.
"Our promotions wont be as competitive this quarter as they were last quarter. There will be less and less retailer promoting computers," he said.
